FOREWORD This Indian Standard (First Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Food Additives Sectional Committee had been approved by the Food and Agriculture Division Council. Carotene is widely distributed in nature. It deri~es its name from carrot (Daucu.s carofa), which contains the colouring principle carotene and is an unsaturated hydrocarbon. Carotene pigment occurs in nature in three important isomeric forms, u, ~ and ~, out of which p-carotene is available in pure form and is also manufactured synthetically. &arx]tene is a precursor of vitamin A and is fat soluble. It is also used as a food COIOLM. This standard is one of a series of Indian Standards Food Adu/terotion R/[/es, 1955. for natural food colours permitted under the Prevention of

This standard was first published in 1966 based on the then existing JECFA Specification for ~-cm-otene. This stanclard is being revised taking into consideration the latest publication for the food colour issued by JECFA and also the latest specifications laid down under the US FDA and the EEC Directives. In this revision the limits for sulphatcd ash and subsidiary colouring matters have been included and requirements for heavy metal contaminants made more stringent to align wilh the international requirements. Requirements lor ~-carotene, food grade have been prescribed undel- the Prevention of F&~dAda/teration Rules, 1955 a)ld due consideration has been given to the rules in the formulation of this standard. Due consideration has aiso been given to the Standards of Weights and A4easlLres (Packaged Comnzodities) Rules, 1977. However, this standard is subject to restrictions imposed under these, wherever applicable. Description Cmmon

SCOPE

1.1 This standard prescribes requirements and methods of sampling and test for O-carotene, food grade, both natural and synthetic. 1.1.1 This standard applies predominantly to all trans isomers of ~-carotene together with minor amounts of other carotenoids. 2 REFERENCES The following standards contain provisions, which through reference in this text constitute provisions of this standard. At the time of publication, the editions indicated were valid. All standards are subject to revision and pirties to agreements based on this standard are encouraged to investigate the possibility of applying the most recent editions of the standards indicated below: IS No. 266:1993 1070:1992 1699:1994 ~qgl : 199g 3 DESCRIPTION 3.1 o-carotene is obtained as clark violet hexagonal prisms when crystallized from benzene-methanol solution; or as red rhombic, almost quadratic plates, from petroleum ether. Title Sulphuric acid -- Specification (third rcvi.sio}?) Reagent grade water (third revision) Methods of sampling and test for food colours (second revision) Food hygiene -- Geneml principles -- Code of practice (.wccvui revision)

3.2 p-carotene exists as red to brownish-red crystals or crystalline powder. Diluted and stabilized forms of carotene include solutions or suspensions of carotene in edible fats or oil, emulsions and water dispersible powders. These preparations may have different cisl trans ratios. 4 REQUIREMENTS 4.1 Spectrophotometric Requirements

Ratio of absorbance of @carotene in cyclohexane (0.2 mg per 100 ml approximately) at 455 nm and 483 nm (Ad5~/A48J) is between 1.14 and 1.19, Solution of &carotene in chloroform on addition of antimony trichloride solution shall give a dark blue colour having maximum absorption at a wave-length of 590 nm. 4,2 The material shall also conform to the requirements given in Table 1. 4.3 The product shall be processed, packed, stored and distributed under hygienic conditions in Iicenced premises (see IS 2491). 5 PACKING, 5.1 Packing The material shall be filled in amber-coloured glass container or any other suitable container sealed under an inert gas as carotene is sensitive to oxygen and light. FOR ASSAYING

PURITY OF J3-CAROTENE A-3 PROCEDURE Accurately weigh about 0.08 g (w) of sample in a 100-nd volumetric flask (VI) and dissolve by shaking briefly with 20 ml pure, acid-free chloroform. Make sure that the solution is clear. Make up to volume by the addition of pure cyclohexane. Pipette 5.0 ml of the solution (v, ) into a 100-m] volumetric flask (VJ and make up to volume with cyclohexane. Similarly, dilute 5.0 ml of this solution (vz) to 100 ml (VJ and measure the absorbance at the absorbance maximum (A)~~n against cyclohexane as a blank,

using 1 cm cells. Calculate the total colouring matters content according to the following formula: Total colouring matter, percent= (AX V, XV2XV,) ,a. v, x V2x w x A;;n

ANNEX B [Table 1, S1 No. (ii)]
DETERMINATION B-1 PROCEDURE Dissolve about 80 mg of sample in 100 ml chloroform. Apply 400 @of this solution as a streak 2 cm from the bottom of a TLC plate (Silica gel 0.25 mm). hnmediately develop the chromatogram with a solvent mixture of 95 parts dichloromethane and 5 parts diethyl ether in a saturated chamber, suitably protected from light, until the solvent front has moved 15 cm above the initial streak. Remove the plate, allow the main part of the solvent to evaporate at room temperature and mark the principal band as well as the bands corresponding to other carotenoids. Remove the silica gel adsorbent that contains the principal band, transfer it to a glass-stoppered 100 ml centrifuge tube and add 40 ml chloroform (Solution 1). Remove the silica gel adsorbent duitcontains the combined bands corresponding to the other carotenoids, transfer it to a glass-stoppered 50 ml OF SUBSIDIARY COLOURING MATTERS (Solution 2).

centrifuge tube and add 20 ml chloroform

Shake the centrifuge tubes by mechanical means for 10 min and centrifuge for 5 min. Dilute 10 ml of Solution 1 to 50 ml with chloroform (Solution 3). Determine, with a suitable spectrophotometer, the absorbance of Solutions 2 and 3 in 1-cm cells at the wavelength maximum about 464 nm, using chloroform as blank. B-2 CALCULATION Percentage of carotenoids other than carotene, percent where Az AT = absorbance = absorbance A, x1OO = A,

of Solution 2, and of Solution 3.
